sentences.why: The rate-decision reasoning (quarter-point hike, higher long-run/neutral dot) is well supported by the GS FOMC recap, but the specific claim being made — the 10-year 'is back at 4.95% this morning' — is a live intraday price with no PDF in the source set covering it. The closest data point, DB's Sept-17 morning note, has the 10yr at 5.00-5.02%, a post-2007 high, not 4.95%, and no file in the given list covers a later date.

This is a claim about the pulse's own prior editorial framing ('this pulse has carried since August 31'), not a claim any research PDF could attest to. No source document discusses TLT or an August 31 dated call.

sentences.span: We now expect the FOMC to deliver a second 25bp hike in October
sentences.why: Goldman's own doc calls for an October second hike (16688) while JPMorgan's doc calls for a December second hike (16690, 'we continue to look for one more hike at the December meeting') — both keep the same eventual destination (see s6), so the actual divergence between the two houses is timing, as stated.

sentences.span: Market pricing of the probability of further hikes this year rose 8pp to 51% for October
sentences.why: Goldman's doc states the October second-hike call explicitly and ties it to the hawkish dot projections and the 51% market pricing for an October hike, matching the sentence.

sentences.span: We continue to look for one more hike at the December meeting, in line with the revised median FOMC expectations
sentences.why: JPM's doc keeps its December second-hike call and separately notes GDP outlook 'revised up a tenth' and unemployment 'revised down to 4.1%' for this year — matching growth-forecasts-up and lower-jobless-rate-path framing.

sentences.span: kept our forecast of the terminal rate unchanged at 3.25-3.5% by adding to the September and December 2027 cuts we already expected a third cut in March 2028
sentences.why: Goldman's 3.25-3.50% terminal range and March-2028 third cut are stated verbatim. JPM's own house terminal figure isn't stated as a separate number in its docs, but both banks' hike calls are explicitly anchored to the same FOMC dot median (Sept dots longer-run 3.2-3.25%), supporting the 'both agree on where rates finish' framing without misattributing a specific figure to JPM.

Multiple documents discuss the Yanbu/Saudi supply disruption qualitatively, but none contains the specific throughput figures (1.1mbd August vs 4mbd April-June, or Saudi production falling to 6.2mbd from 10.9mbd in February) anywhere in the source set.

sentences.span: EU gas storage is a little over 68% full, well below the seasonal 5-year average of 84%
sentences.why: ING's commodities feed gives the exact 68%/84% figures. Diesel margins are corroborated by the same doc's 'ICE gasoil crack remains above $80/bbl and near record levels' plus a separate note that retail diesel 'recently hit a record high above $6 a gallon.'

sentences.span: Stronger AI safeguards may reshape competition, but the proposals so far do not establish that the AI capex cycle is ending
sentences.why: UBS's stance is exactly this: AI-linked stocks sold off on the pacing-call news, but UBS argues the capex cycle isn't ending and tells investors with concentrated AI holdings to rebalance toward a broader AI value-chain mix — a rotation within the theme, not an exit.

There is exactly one Bank of America-sourced document in the set (16570, a CIO macro/AI-singularity outlook letter) and it contains no S&P 500 target, no 7,800 figure, and no rotation calls. No other document mentions a BofA 12-month S&P target.

No document discusses a 'value basket' or the historical record of cheap stocks outperforming expensive ones during Fed tightening. The one BofA doc in the set favors Value over Growth for a different reason (valuation difficulty for long-duration assets amid higher real yields), not this record/tightening framing.
Neither AHR nor WELL (nor the $71/$292 targets) appears anywhere in the source set.

No document states a 'nearly six months without a 5% pullback' claim, an earnings-concentration-at-a-record claim, or an $8 trillion cash-on-sidelines/money-market figure. Trillion-dollar figures found in the set are unrelated (AI capex spend estimates, asset-manager AUM).
No document discusses a mechanical support flow 'rolling off Friday' — no mention of options expiration, quad-witching, or OpEx tied to that dynamic anywhere in the set.

No document attributes a $9.9 billion dealer net-long gamma figure to Bank of America (the only BofA doc in the set doesn't discuss options positioning at all). The only gamma discussions found are Goldman's pre-FOMC equity-derivatives note (describing street gamma as 'pretty flat', not a specific net-long dollar figure) and a Treasury-options gamma exhibit, neither of which matches.
